To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the complexity of policy iteration in Markov decision processes with a finite number of states and actions grows polynomially in the number of possible policies, and that this complexity bound is tight.
the number of iterations of policy iteration is at most exponential in the number (or equivalently, the sum of logarithms) of the number of states, actions, or policies.
the worst-case number of iterations required for PI to converge to an optimal policy is O(n 3 ) in the case of a discounted MDP with n states, and O(n 4 ) in the case that the MDP is not discounted.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have proved the first non-trivial upper bounds on the worst-case complexity of PI and that we have shown how the complexity is determined by the number of policies that are “good enough” to reach the optimal policy.
PI can be made to converge in a number of iterations that is polynomial in the size of the state space.
we have shown that PI can be very efficient, but that the efficiency of PI is not a property of MD Ps.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of iterations needed by PI depends not just on the size of the state space, but on the structure of the optimal policy.
PI does not necessarily converge in a greedy manner: it may visit policies that are far from the optimal policy.
PI can be viewed as an algorithm for computing the fixed point of a non-linear function, and that this fixed point can be found in polynomial time.
